newsitem.title: THAILAND: Bangkok property values to fall - real estate firm.
newsitem.headline: Bangkok property values to fall - real estate firm.

text.p: Bangkok property prices and rentals are set to fall by around 10 percent during 1997 in many sectors of the Thai capital's troubled property market, property firm Richard Ellis forecast on Thursday.

Housing, office, freehold condominium and serviced apartment sectors of the market are set to lose between five to 11 percent of their capital or rental values this year as oversupply continues to erode prices, senior company executives told reporters.
Top quality city centre locations are likely to be less affected by declining prices while retail, industrial and apartment sectors, though under pressure, are likely to hold their value, they said.

"Clearly there is a serious concern and a lack of confidence in the property market and in terms of transactions and movements it has had a very depressing effect," managing director David Simister said.
However, the firm ruled out a dramatic collapse in the market as demand in most sectors was strong during the first quarter and should continue at high levels during the rest of year, he said.

"Given the size and volume of Bangkok's property market, a market like Bangkok's just doesn't come to a stop because people feel property is something that is no longer rapidly appreciating in value," he said.
The firm said its forecasts were based on economic growth projections of five to six percent in 1997.
In the housing sector, where between 300,000-600,000 units are said to be empty, the firm said prices fell by five percent during the first quarter.

But the 600,000 figure probably overestimates the scale of the problems and the firm believed market prices would show a decline of approximately 10 percent this year, research manager Philip Finch said.
Office values are predicted to fall 11 percent, while office rentals were likely to decline by between five and 10 percent, he said.
Room rates in the serviced apartment sector are forecast to fall by 10 percent or more. Freehold condominium prices are set to fall by 11 percent, Finch said.
